summary: Draft watchdog sibling record. `Win32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` sits under the same `Session Manager\\Power` lane as the validated watchdog timeout pair, is absent by default on the clean baseline, has a current-build Unicode string hit in `ntoskrnl.exe`, resolves to a live `nt!PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` watchdog-family global on the KVM current build, and now has both a canonical PDB-backed Ghidra structural pass and a broader KVM local-KD seeding sweep. Together they show a narrower result than the earlier draft wording: the current build still carries the sibling, the live global currently reads `0`, but the direct named wrapper path is not the reader, the canonical full-analysis Ghidra pass recovered no direct or bounded xrefs, and the wider watchdog/bugcheck symbol sweep did not reveal a current-build registry seeding caller. This keeps the record alive as an adjacent watchdog-family global with unproven registry semantics, not as the strongest next tweak candidate.

setting.name: Win32 Callout Watchdog Bugcheck Enabled
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a low-level watchdog-related value under Session Manager Power. On the current clean baseline, the parent key exists but the value is not configured.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect this value when tracing watchdog behavior around Session Manager power initialization and callout handling.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value is kernel-adjacent, boot-relevant, and still unproven as an end-user tweak. Evidence is good enough to keep it in the research queue as a watchdog-family adjacent global, but not good enough to apply, recommend, or even treat as the strongest next watchdog candidate without a real seeding or read path.
setting.professional_notes: The current repo evidence says `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Session Manager\\Power\\Win32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` is absent by default on the clean baseline while the parent path exists. A later targeted current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit in `C:\\Windows\\System32\\ntoskrnl.exe`. A later KVM local-KD symbol sweep resolved a live `nt!PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` global alongside `PopWatchdogInit`, `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout`, `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout`, and `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog`, which proved the sibling still exists in the current watchdog-family symbol surface. A direct KVM local-KD follow-up then showed that `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog` uses `PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds`, builds a watchdog callback packet around `PopWin32CalloutWatchdogCallback`, calls `ZwPowerInformation`, and then invokes `PsInvokeWin32Callout`; the same pass read `PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled = 0` live, but did not show that wrapper reading the target global. The new canonical PDB-backed Ghidra full-analysis pass confirmed that the exact value-name string still exists in `ntoskrnl.exe`, but recovered zero direct or bounded xrefs from that string. The new broader KVM local-KD seed sweep then widened the search across watchdog/bugcheck symbols and helper disassembly, but still did not reveal a target-specific setter, copy helper, or registry seeding caller for the global. The only proven current-build registry helper path in this neighborhood remains the generic power reader chain `PopReadUlongPowerKey -> PopReadRegKeyValue -> ZwOpenKey / ZwQueryValueKey`, and the directly observed timeout selector still reads `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout` and `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout`, not this sibling. The right interpretation is now narrower: this is an adjacent watchdog-family global with unproven registry semantics on the current build, not the strongest un-packaged watchdog tweak lead. Absent a new runtime or documentation lead, this sibling should stop taking priority over stronger watchdog lanes.

decision.why: The candidate is still real enough for a schema-backed draft: it has baseline path/value evidence, a current-build kernel string hit, a live watchdog-family global on the current build, a direct KD disassembly proving that the obvious Win32 callout wrapper is not the direct reader, and a later broader KD seeding sweep plus canonical full-analysis Ghidra pass. Those later passes narrowed the claim instead of strengthening it: they did not find a current-build registry seeding path, exact registry-read proof, documented semantics, or safe non-default value mapping, so further escalation should wait for a new runtime or documentation lead.
